definition: Bilk means to cheat someone out of money.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word bilk. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know bilk should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The ticket broker bilked hundreds of fans, collecting full price for seats in rows the stadium did not contain.
Shortchange is milder than bilk — a shortchanged customer is out a few coins at the register, more insult than injury.
Fleece goes further than bilk: a bilked victim loses money, but a fleeced one is stripped bare, the way a sheep loses its whole coat in one shearing.

To swindle is to cheat someone by scheme, big or small — the everyday word for the whole family of cons. Bilk narrows the target to money: to bilk someone is to cheat them out of cash, typically by charging for something that was never real.

Defraud is the formal, courtroom term for deliberately taking money by deception — it is the word an indictment uses. Bilk means the same money-cheating but lives in headlines and everyday speech: quicker, more vivid, and reaching plenty of small-time tricks no prosecutor would ever pursue.
hands money back instead of taking it
settles a debt honestly and in full

Because bilk began as gaming slang rather than as a Latin or Greek root, it never grew a family — no prefix, no suffix, no cousins. If another word looks like bilk, it is probably milk, and the two have nothing to do with each other.
Bilk means to cheat someone out of money.
The clinic's billing office bilked the insurance company for a decade, charging for therapy sessions on days when the building was locked.
Bilk is specifically about money slipping away through cheating.
Overcharging is greedy but open, and to shortchange is to skim a little — to bilk is to take money for something that was never real: sessions never held, seats that never existed.
Bilk is a compact, headline-flavored verb for cheating people out of money — it wants a victim and a sum.
Swindle works almost anywhere bilk does; defraud is what the indictment will say.
And when the price was merely outrageous rather than stolen, overcharge is the honest word.

The Riverbend Wellness Club opened its sales office before it opened anything else.
For eight months, residents paid founding-member fees for a lap pool, a sauna, and a rooftop track that existed only in the brochures.
When the county finally posted a stop-work order on the empty lot, members compared notes and realized the club had bilked them out of nearly ninety thousand dollars.
The manager insisted the delays were normal.
But investigators found no permits, no contractor, and no plans on file — nothing behind the drawings but a rented trailer.
For the members, the sting was less the money than the memory of paying, month after month, for a pool that was never going to hold water.
